header: Petitioner by: M/s Muhammad Wajid Hussain
Respondent No.4/CDA by: Ms. Saadia Shahzadi, Advocate.
Applicant in objection case Mr. Riffat Hussain Malik,
body: INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J-. Through the instant writ petition, the petitioner impugns the order dated 02.03.2023 (“Impugned Order”), passed by the learned Civil Judge 1 st Class, West-Islamabad (“Trial Court”) whereby application under Section 12(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”) filed by respondent No.2, Ishtiaq Hussain Shah Kazmi, against the judgment and decree dated 03.11.2017 was allowed and the said judgment and decree was set-aside.

2. Brief facts of the instant writ petition are that the petitioner filed a suit for Specific Performance of an agreement to sell dated 25.04.2017 against respondents No.3 and 4, which was decreed on 03.11.2017 on the basis of the statement made by respondent No.3. Consequently, Plot No.173, measuring 30×70, situated in Sector F- 11/4, Islamabad, was transferred in the name of the petitioner on 02.12.2019. Subsequently, respondent No.2 filed an application under Section 12(2) CPC, alleging that he had purchased the disputed plot from Amna Bibi, mother of respondent No.3, on 09.08.2003, and that a suit for specific performance filed by him in respect of the same plot 2 W.P No.1461/2023.

was already pending before the Civil Court. He further asserted that respondent No.3 had no right to sell the disputed plot and had procured the decree in favour of the petitioner through misrepresentation. During the pendency of the said proceedings, the petitioner was proceeded against ex-parte vide order dated 22.04.2021, against which he filed an application for setting aside the ex-parte proceedings on 27.05.2021. However, without deciding the said application or allowing the petitioner to submit a written reply to the application under Section 12(2) CPC, the learned Trial Court recorded the conceding statement of respondent No.3 on 07.12.2022 and, vide the Impugned Order allowed the application under Section 12(2) CPC, thereby setting aside the judgment and decree dated 03.11.2017.

3. The learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the Impugned Order is unlawful and has been passed in violation of the principles of natural justice, as the learned Trial Court decided the application under Section 12(2) CPC without first deciding the petitioner’s pending application for setting aside the ex-parte proceedings or providing him an opportunity of hearing. It was argued that respondent No.2 had no lawful claim over the disputed plot, as his alleged agreement dated 09.08.2003 was executed with Amna Bibi, who was never allotted the plot and died on 13.03.2017, whereas the plot was subsequently allotted to respondent No.3 on 26.09.2017 and lawfully transferred to the petitioner pursuant to a Court decree, and the alleged earlier agreement did not identify any specific plot and was therefore unenforceable. It was also argued that the learned Trial Court also wrongly relied upon another disputed agreement dated 18.03.2017, which was neither mentioned in respondent No.2’s amended plaint nor made the basis of his suit and that the said agreement was subsequently prepared through collusion between respondents No.2 and 3 to defeat his lawful rights. It was further argued that the disputed agreements and allegations of fraud required proper evidence and could not be decided merely on the conceding statement of respondent No.3 without hearing the petitioner and that the learned Trial Court has also failed to consider 3 W.P No.1461/2023.

the relevant case law and decided the main application on a date fixed for hearing the petitioner’s pending application, therefore, the Impugned Order, being contrary to law, evidence and the right to a fair hearing, is liable to be set aside.

4. I have heard learned counsel for the petitioner and carefully examined the available record, including the documents produced through CM No.3 of 2025. Despite opportunities, respondents No.2 and 3 did not appear to contest the present proceedings and were consequently proceeded against ex-parte. The principal questions requiring determination are whether the learned Trial Court was justified in setting aside the consent decree dated 03.11.2017 without first deciding the petitioner’s pending application for restoration of his right to contest, and what effect the subsequent dismissal of respondent No.2’s suit for specific performance has upon the Impugned Order.

5. Before examining the merits, it is appropriate to consider the scope and purpose of Section 12(2), CPC. This provision provides a remedy to a person, who challenges the validity of a judgment, decree or order on the ground of fraud, misrepresentation or want of jurisdiction. This provision aims to prevent a party from retaining the benefit of a judicial decision obtained through unlawful means. However, the mere allegation of fraud or misrepresentation is not sufficient to invalidate a decree. The party seeking such relief must establish the necessary facts through reliable and legally admissible evidence. A decree passed by a competent Court carries legal effect unless it is set aside in accordance with law. Therefore, proceedings under Section 12(2), CPC cannot be treated as a substitute for a regular appeal or as a means of reopening a concluded matter merely because another person claims an interest in the property.

6. It is equally settled that the right to a fair hearing is an essential requirement of judicial proceedings. Article 10-A of the Constitution guarantees the right to due process, while the principles of natural justice require that no person be condemned without a reasonable 4 W.P No.1461/2023.

opportunity to present his case. Where an application seeking to set aside ex-parte proceedings is pending, particularly in a matter involving valuable property rights, the Court is required to consider and decide that application in accordance with law before finally determining the main proceedings in a manner, which may prejudice the absent party. The failure to do so may amount to a material procedural irregularity where it deprives the affected party of an effective opportunity to contest the claim.

7. In the present case, the record reflects that the petitioner was proceeded against ex-parte on 22.04.2021, who filed an application for setting aside that order on 27.05.2021. The said application remained undecided when the learned Trial Court proceeded to decide the main application under Section 12(2), CPC on 02.03.2023. This approach was not legally justified. The petitioner was the beneficiary of the decree under challenge, and any order setting aside that decree directly affected his rights. He was, therefore, entitled to a meaningful opportunity to contest the allegations of fraud and misrepresentation. The learned Trial Court ought to have first determined whether sufficient grounds existed for setting aside the ex-parte proceedings and thereafter proceeded with the main application in accordance with law. By deciding the substantive controversy without resolving the pending application, the learned Trial Court deprived the petitioner of an effective opportunity of hearing.

8. Another important aspect is that the Impugned Order was substantially based upon the statement of respondent No.3, Zeeshan Ali, who had earlier appeared before the Civil Court and consented to the decree in favour of the petitioner. A statement made by one party may be relevant against that party, but it cannot automatically determine the rights of another person who disputes its correctness. The petitioner had acquired rights under the decree dated 03.11.2017, and those rights could not lawfully be defeated merely on the basis of a subsequent conceding statement of respondent No.3 without affording 5 W.P No.1461/2023.

the petitioner an opportunity to challenge that statement and produce evidence in support of his own claim. The allegations concerning the earlier agreements and the alleged collusion between the parties required proper judicial examination, not acceptance solely on the basis of a concession.

9. The subsequent developments brought on record during the pendency of the present petition are of even greater significance. Through CM No.3 of 2025, the petitioner produced documents showing that the suit for specific performance instituted by respondent No.2 on the basis of the alleged earlier agreement had already been dismissed by the competent Civil Court on 21.04.2025. It is also brought on record that respondent No.2 did not file any appeal against that judgment. Thus, the decision dismissing his suit has remained unchallenged. Respondent No.2 has also failed to appear before this Court to dispute these subsequent developments or to demonstrate that any enforceable right in his favour still survives.

10. The legal effect of this subsequent development cannot be ignored. The principal foundation of respondent No.2’s application under Section 12(2), CPC was his assertion that he possessed an earlier contractual right over the disputed plot arising from the agreement dated 09.08.2003 and its alleged continuation dated 18.03.2017. He maintained that the decree obtained by the petitioner interfered with his rights, which were already the subject of his pending suit for specific performance. However, that suit has now been dismissed, and the dismissal has remained unchallenged. Consequently, respondent No.2 has failed to establish the contractual entitlement upon which he principally relied to challenge the petitioner’s decree.

11. It is important to clarify that the dismissal of a separate suit for specific performance does not, in every case, automatically establish the validity of another decree or remove an independently proved allegation of fraud. A decree obtained through fraud or misrepresentation cannot be protected merely because a competing 6 W.P No.1461/2023.

contractual claim has failed. Nevertheless, the effect of the dismissal must be examined in the circumstances of each case. In the present matter, respondent No.2’s challenge rested substantially on his alleged earlier contractual entitlement and the pendency of proceedings for its enforcement. Once those proceedings ended in dismissal, and no independent basis sufficient to sustain the order under Section 12(2) CPC remained established on the available record, the foundation of the Impugned Order was materially weakened.

12. The Court is also required to consider that the decree dated 03.11.2017 had already been acted upon. The disputed plot was transferred in the petitioner’s name on 02.12.2019 pursuant to the decree. The record does not show that respondent No. 2 or respondent No. 3 separately challenged the said transfer before the competent forum. Although the transfer of property pursuant to a decree does not, by itself, prevent a lawful challenge to that decree, it remains a relevant circumstance in determining the rights already created and the consequences of setting aside the decree. In the absence of any successful challenge to the transfer and following the dismissal of respondent No.2’s suit, the available record provides no sufficient legal basis to continue depriving the petitioner of the benefit of the decree passed in his favour.

13. The principle governing the consideration of subsequent events is that a Court may take notice of material developments occurring during the pendency of proceedings, where those developments directly affect the controversy and are necessary for granting effective relief. Judicial proceedings should not be decided in disregard of an admitted or established change in circumstances, which has substantially altered the rights or claims of the parties. The purpose of considering such developments is to avoid unnecessary litigation and ensure that the relief granted corresponds with the existing legal position. In the present case, the dismissal of respondent No.2’s suit on 21.04.2025 is 7 W.P No.1461/2023.
directly relevant because the earlier contractual claim formed the principal basis of his challenge to the petitioner’s decree.

14. It is further significant that respondents No.2 and 3, despite being parties to the present proceedings, have not appeared to contest the petition or challenge the documents produced through CM No.3 of 2025. Their absence does not automatically entitle the petitioner to relief, as the Court remains obligated to examine the legality of the Impugned Order. However, where the petitioner has produced relevant judicial documents showing the dismissal of the competing suit and those documents remain unrebutted, the Court is entitled to consider their legal effect. In the circumstances, no material has been brought before this Court demonstrating that respondent No.2 continues to possess an enforceable right, which would justify maintaining the order setting aside the petitioner’s decree.

15. The jurisdiction of this Court under Article 199 of the Constitution is supervisory in nature and is ordinarily exercised to correct jurisdictional errors, material illegalities and violations of fundamental principles of law. This Court does not sit as a regular appellate forum over every factual finding of a subordinate Court. However, constitutional interference is justified where the Impugned Order has been passed in violation of the right to a fair hearing, where material procedural safeguards have been disregarded, or where the decision cannot be sustained in view of the established legal position. The present case falls within these principles because the learned Trial Court decided the application under Section 12(2) CPC without first deciding the petitioner’s pending application for setting aside the exparte proceedings, relied upon the subsequent concession of respondent No.3 without providing the petitioner an effective opportunity to contest it, and the principal contractual claim relied upon by respondent No.2 has subsequently failed.
16. The learned Trial Court has failed to follow the proper procedure and deprived the petitioner of a reasonable opportunity to defend the 8 W.P No.1461/2023.

decree obtained in his favour. Moreover, the subsequent dismissal of respondent No.2’s suit for specific performance on 21.04.2025 has removed the principal basis upon which he asserted a competing right over the disputed property. The decree dated 03.11.2017 had already been executed through transfer of the plot in the petitioner’s name, and no successful independent challenge to that transfer has been shown. In these circumstances, maintaining the Impugned Order would serve no lawful purpose and would unnecessarily prejudice the petitioner’s rights.

17. In view of the foregoing discussion, the present writ petition is allowed. The Impugned Order passed by the learned Trial Court on the application under Section 12(2) CPC, is hereby set aside, and the said application is accordingly dismissed. Consequently, judgment and decree dated 03.11.2017, passed in favour of the petitioner in the suit for specific performance of the agreement dated 25.04.2017, are restored. The transfer of Plot No.173, measuring 30×70 feet, situated in Sector F-11/4, Islamabad, effected in favour of the petitioner pursuant to the said decree, shall remain undisturbed.
(INAAM AMEEN MINHAS)
